# code-generation

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenAPI Generator overview and workflow — https://nordicapis.com/introduction-to-openapi-generator/ ; OpenAPI Generator usage in practice — https://apidog.com/blog/openapi-generator-5/ ; OpenAPI Specification v3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0
- **Depends on:** dependency-management, dev-environment
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** code is produced mechanically from a machine-readable source — an OpenAPI description (clients, server stubs, types), a database schema (ORM models), or project templates (scaffolding) — and whenever generated output already in the repo changes.
- **Do NOT use when:** the code is written by hand, however repetitive it feels; hand-written code belongs to its owning skill. Do not use generation to produce a finished-looking feature: a generated scaffold is a starting shape, not an implementation.

## Rules

1. **DX-041 — Named source of truth.** Every generated artifact traces to one machine-readable source committed in the repo — an OpenAPI description, a schema, or a template set. The generation command and its source are recorded in the project config; output with no named source is deleted, not adopted.
2. **DX-042 — Never hand-edit output.** A change to generated code is made in the source or the template, then regenerated. A hand edit in a generated file is a defect, even if the edit itself is correct.
3. **DX-043 — Generated header.** Every generated file carries the standard header naming the generator, the generator version, and the source file it was generated from. A file in a generated directory without the header is flagged, not assumed hand-written.
4. **DX-044 — Generator pinned.** The generator and its exact version are declared in the dependency manifest and lockfile like any other dependency. Generating with an unpinned or locally different generator version is not permitted.
5. **DX-045 — Deterministic regeneration.** The same source plus the same generator version produces byte-identical output on any machine. Generators that embed timestamps, absolute paths, or unordered iteration are configured or wrapped until the output is stable.
6. **DX-046 — One output rule, stated.** Generated output is either committed (so a source change shows as an output diff in review) or built fresh in CI and never committed. The project states which rule applies; a mixture of both is drift waiting to happen.
7. **DX-047 — Source reviewed like code.** The spec or schema change goes through the same review as a code change. Generation is never a route for an unreviewed API or data-model change to enter the codebase disguised as a mechanical update.
8. **DX-048 — Generated code passes every gate.** Generated code is linted, type-checked, and tested by the same pipeline as hand-written code. "Generated" is not an exemption from any project gate.
9. **DX-049 — Scaffolds fail loudly.** A generated stub that is not yet implemented throws an explicit not-implemented error or carries a failing test. It never returns canned data that callers or UI can mistake for real behavior.
10. **DX-050 — Template overrides are minimal and documented.** Custom templates are versioned with the project. Where a stock template is overridden, the override is as small as possible and the reason is recorded next to the template.
11. **DX-051 — Regeneration runs in CI.** CI regenerates from the committed source and diffs against the committed output (where output is committed). Any difference fails the build; drift is never merged and fixed later.
12. **DX-052 — Hand-written logic lives outside generated files.** Custom behavior goes in files the generator never overwrites — separate modules, registered hooks, or the generator's documented extension points. If no extension point exists, wrap the generated code; do not fork it by editing it.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-021 — The hand-edited generated file.** Banned: editing generated output directly instead of changing the source or template and regenerating. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: change the OpenAPI description or the template, regenerate, and commit source and output together. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-022 — The unmarked generated file.** Banned: generated output shipped without the generated-file header naming generator, version, and source. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Instead: configure the generator to emit the standard header on every file, and fail the header scan (G-DX-023) on any file missing it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-023 — The canned-data stub.** Banned: a generated endpoint or function that returns sample data, an empty success, or a hardcoded result while callers and UI treat the feature as working. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Instead: leave the stub throwing an explicit not-implemented error until the real implementation replaces it (DX-049). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-024 — The unpinned generator.** Banned: generating from a globally installed, latest, or otherwise unrecorded generator version. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: pin the generator and its version in the manifest and lockfile (DX-044) and generate only through the project's recorded command. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-025 — The gate-exempt generated directory.** Banned: excluding generated code from lint, type checking, or tests "because it is generated." Defeats: DET-CODE-004. Instead: run the full pipeline over generated code like any other code (DX-048); fix failures at the source or template. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-021 — Drift check.** Verifies: DX-042, DX-045, DX-051. Check: automated — in CI, regenerate from the committed source into a temporary directory (`<generate command> --output /tmp/regen`) and run `diff -r /tmp/regen <generated dir>`; also run `git status --porcelain <generated dir>` after a local regeneration. Pass: zero differences. Fail: block the merge; the fix is made in the source or template, never by committing the drift. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-022 — Determinism check.** Verifies: DX-044, DX-045. Check: automated — run the recorded generation command twice in clean checkouts and compare `find <generated dir> -type f -exec sha256sum {} +` output between the runs. Pass: identical hash lists. Fail: block; find and remove the nondeterminism (timestamp, path, ordering) before any output is committed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-023 — Header scan.** Verifies: DX-043. Check: automated — `grep -rL "<generated-header marker>" <generated dir>` returns no files, and a grep for manual-edit markers in generated files returns nothing. Pass: every generated file carries the header naming generator, version, and source. Fail: block; regenerate with the header configured. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-024 — Full pipeline over generated code.** Verifies: DX-048. Check: automated — run the project's lint, type check, and test suite with no exclusion for generated directories. Pass: all three pass. Fail: block; the correction goes into the source or template and is regenerated, not patched in the output. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-025 — Stub honesty check.** Verifies: DX-049. Check: automated plus spot check — grep generated stubs for canned return bodies (literal arrays/objects returned from operations with no implementation), and exercise one unimplemented generated endpoint. Pass: every unimplemented operation throws an explicit not-implemented error; no generated stub returns sample data as if real. Fail: block the feature from being presented as working until implemented. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Edit the source, never the output.
- Same source, same generator, same bytes — on any machine.
- If it is generated, it is marked, pinned, and gated.
- A stub that lies is worse than a stub that throws.
- Drift in CI is a failed build, not a follow-up task.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every generated artifact names its committed source of truth (DX-041).
- [ ] Generator and version are pinned in the manifest and lockfile (DX-044).
- [ ] Drift check passes: regeneration matches committed output exactly (G-DX-021).
- [ ] Determinism check passes: two clean regenerations are byte-identical (G-DX-022).
- [ ] Every generated file carries the standard header (G-DX-023).
- [ ] Lint, type check, and tests pass with no generated-directory exclusions (G-DX-024).
- [ ] No unimplemented stub returns canned data; stubs throw not-implemented (G-DX-025).
- [ ] Template overrides are minimal, versioned, and documented (DX-050).

# dependency-management

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Dependabot version updates — https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-your-supply-chain/secure-your-dependencies/configure-version-updates ; Renovate npm manager and lockfile maintenance — https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/manager/npm/
- **Depends on:** dev-environment (toolchain pins the installs run under), tech-debt (debt register holds stale-update reasons)
- **Feeds into:** dependency-safety (D7 — receives routed advisories), versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** adding, updating, pinning, or removing a dependency; configuring update automation; reviewing a change that touches the manifest or the lockfile.
- **Do NOT use when:** responding to a published vulnerability or a compromised package — that is D7's dependency-safety, which owns advisory triage, patch SLAs, and incident response. This skill owns the everyday discipline of choosing, pinning, and updating dependencies; it routes advisories to D7 and never runs a parallel security process.

## Rules

1. **DX-061 — The lockfile is committed and canonical.** The lockfile is version-controlled next to the manifest. A change that edits one without the other is incomplete and does not merge.
2. **DX-062 — Installs are frozen and reproducible.** Local setup and CI install from the lockfile in frozen mode (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, or the ecosystem equivalent). An install that modifies the lockfile is a failed install, not a fix.
3. **DX-063 — Every new direct dependency is justified in one line.** The change description states what the package does, why the standard library and the existing dependencies do not cover it, and its maintenance status. No justification, no merge.
4. **DX-064 — Update automation is configured in the repo.** A committed `.github/dependabot.yml` or `renovate.json` drives updates: minor and patch grouped, majors individual, security updates ungrouped and immediate. The config validates against its schema.
5. **DX-065 — Updates land in small, reviewed batches.** Grouped minor/patch updates merge as small batches; a major update is its own change. A single change never bumps many unrelated packages at once.
6. **DX-066 — Read the changelog before a major update.** The change description names the breaking changes from the release notes and the code changes they required. "Tests pass" alone is not a major-update review.
7. **DX-067 — Version ranges are deliberate.** Applications pin exact versions. Caret ranges appear only in published libraries where the ecosystem convention makes them the consumer contract. Wildcard ranges are prohibited (BAN-DX-032).
8. **DX-068 — No stale update without a recorded reason.** No update PR or report entry stays unaddressed past the project's stated window (default 30 days) unless the debt register records why and when it will be taken.
9. **DX-069 — Dead and duplicate dependencies are removed.** A package nothing imports is deleted from the manifest in the same change that removed its last use; two packages serving one job collapse to one. Removal is part of the work, not a later cleanup.
10. **DX-070 — The manifest stays coherent.** Every manifest entry is imported, or its build/plugin role is documented in the manifest's config; every import resolves to a declared entry. Transitive packages are never imported directly.
11. **DX-071 — Advisories route to D7, currency stays here.** Audit findings are handed to dependency-safety for triage and patching priority; this skill's job is only to keep versions current enough that D7's patches are small. Never sit on a known advisory because "the update is scheduled."
12. **DX-072 — An update merges only on a green suite.** The full test suite passes in CI on the updated tree, installed frozen from the updated lockfile, before any update change merges.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-031 — Uncommitted or casually regenerated lockfile.** Banned: deleting the lockfile and regenerating it inside an unrelated change, or leaving it out of version control. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: regenerate the lockfile only in a dedicated update change whose diff is the review. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-032 — Wildcard or `latest` version ranges.** Banned: `"*"`, `latest`, or an open range in any manifest entry. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: pin the exact version for applications; use a caret range only for a published library per DX-067. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-033 — Manifest and lockfile changed out of step.** Banned: a change that edits the manifest without the lockfile, or the lockfile without the manifest. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: generate both in the same local install and commit them together (DX-061). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-034 — Duplicate libraries for one job.** Banned: two packages serving the same purpose in one codebase (two date libraries, two HTTP clients, two validation libraries). Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: use the package already in the tree; if the new one is genuinely better, migrate fully and remove the old in the same change. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-035 — Hand-edited lockfile.** Banned: editing lockfile entries by hand to force a version, instead of changing the manifest and letting the package manager resolve. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: express the constraint in the manifest (pin, override field) and regenerate the lockfile with the package manager. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-031 — Frozen-lockfile install.** Verifies: DX-061, DX-062. Check: in a clean CI checkout run `npm ci` (or the ecosystem frozen equivalent), then `git status --porcelain`. Pass: install exits 0 and the lockfile shows no modification. Fail: block merge; the manifest/lockfile pair is regenerated and recommitted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-032 — Production audit threshold.** Verifies: DX-071. Check: run `npm audit --production` / `pip-audit` / ecosystem equivalent in CI. Pass: no high or critical advisories in production dependencies; any finding is logged and routed to D7 dependency-safety the same day. Fail: block release until D7 triages. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-033 — Update-bot config present and valid.** Verifies: DX-064. Check: assert `.github/dependabot.yml` or `renovate.json` exists and validate it (`npx renovate-config-validator` or the Dependabot schema check). Pass: file present, schema-valid, majors ungrouped, security updates ungrouped. Fail: block; add or fix the config before further dependency work. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-034 — Stale-dependency report.** Verifies: DX-065, DX-068. Check: run `npm outdated` (or equivalent) and list direct dependencies more than one major behind, or with an update unaddressed past the 30-day window. Pass: the list is empty, or every entry has a debt-register reason with a take-by date. Fail: warn and register the items before the next feature change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-035 — Manifest coherence scan.** Verifies: DX-069, DX-070. Check: run `npx depcheck` (or equivalent) and diff the import list against the manifest. Pass: no unused and no missing dependencies, except build/plugin packages documented in config. Fail: block; remove or declare before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- The manifest is the intent; the lockfile is the truth.
- Every dependency is inventory: justified, pinned, pruned.
- Majors land one at a time, changelog in hand.
- Security response belongs to D7; currency belongs here.
- If nothing imports it, it does not stay.

## Checklist

- [ ] Lockfile committed, and a frozen install leaves it unchanged (G-DX-031).
- [ ] Every new direct dependency carries its one-line justification (DX-063).
- [ ] Update-bot config exists, validates, and keeps majors and security updates ungrouped (G-DX-033).
- [ ] No update is past the stale window without a debt-register reason (G-DX-034).
- [ ] Coherence scan is clean: nothing unused, nothing missing, no transitive imports (G-DX-035).
- [ ] Major updates landed individually with their breaking changes named (DX-065, DX-066).
- [ ] Full suite green on the updated tree before merge (DX-072).

# dev-environment

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://containers.dev/implementors/json_reference/ ; https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/ ; https://12factor.net/config
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: setup is derived from the project's own repo (its manifests, version pins, and environment variables) so a fresh machine can run it; it is a starting-point skill and consumes no other skill's output. It feeds monorepo-tooling and dependency-management.
- **Feeds into:** monorepo-tooling, dependency-management

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project is created or handed over; a new machine, container, or CI runner must reach a running app; setup instructions, tool versions, or environment variables are being written or changed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which versions to bump in an existing dependency set (use dependency-management), how releases are numbered (use versioning), or how production is deployed (use D6 deployment skills) — this skill covers the local development environment only.

## Rules

1. **DX-001 — One bootstrap command.** Exactly one documented command (e.g. `make setup`, `npm run setup`, or `mise install` plus the install step) takes a clean clone to a running app with the test suite passing. Any second manual step is a defect in the setup, not a README footnote.
2. **DX-002 — One pin file.** Every runtime and CLI tool version is declared exactly once, in one committed pin file (`mise.toml`, `.tool-versions`, or the ecosystem equivalent). No other file restates a tool version.
3. **DX-003 — Exact pins, never "latest".** The pin file and dependency manifests carry exact versions for tools and application dependencies. Floating references (`latest`, `*`, unpinned "current LTS") are not permitted anywhere in setup instructions or config.
4. **DX-004 — Lockfile committed, installs frozen.** The dependency lockfile is committed, and local and CI installs run in frozen/CI mode (`npm ci`, `--frozen-lockfile`, or equivalent) so an install never silently rewrites the resolved set.
5. **DX-005 — `.env.example` is complete.** Every variable the code reads appears in `.env.example` with a placeholder value and a one-line purpose note. A variable read by code but missing from the example file is a defect.
6. **DX-006 — Placeholders only.** Example files contain only obviously non-functional values (`change-me`, `sk_test_...`, reserved example hosts). No real secret, token, or connection string appears in any committed file, example or otherwise.
7. **DX-007 — Config fails fast.** The app validates required configuration at startup and exits non-zero, naming each missing or malformed variable. There is no silent fallback to a default environment, host, or credential.
8. **DX-008 — Setup is idempotent.** Running the bootstrap command a second time changes nothing and breaks nothing: no duplicate installs, no clobbered local config, no appended duplicates in generated files.
9. **DX-009 — CI runs the same pins.** CI installs the toolchain from the same pin file and the dependencies from the same lockfile as a laptop. A CI-only version override is drift, treated as a defect under DX-002.
10. **DX-010 — Services are declared, not hand-started.** When the app needs backing services (database, cache, queue), they are declared in `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` and/or a compose file committed with the project, and the bootstrap starts them. "Start Postgres locally first" is not a setup step.
11. **DX-011 — Config comes from the environment.** Per-deploy values arrive as environment variables (Twelve-Factor Factor III), strictly separate from code. Code contains no `if (environment === "prod")` branches selecting hardcoded URLs, hosts, or credentials.
12. **DX-012 — README references, never restates.** The README names the bootstrap command and links the pin file and `.env.example`. It restates no version numbers and no variable lists, so there is exactly one place each can drift from.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-001 — Real secret in an example or config file.** Banned: a working API key, password, or connection string committed in `.env.example`, a config sample, or source. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Instead: placeholder values only, per DX-006. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-002 — Floating tool versions.** Banned: setup instructions or manifests that install `latest`, a wildcard range, or an unpinned "current LTS" for any runtime or CLI tool. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: pin the exact version in the pin file and install from it, per DX-002 and DX-003. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-003 — Setup steps outside the bootstrap.** Banned: any required setup step that lives only in a wiki, chat message, or a human's memory instead of the bootstrap command. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: fold the step into the bootstrap command, per DX-001. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-004 — Silent default to production.** Banned: a fallback that points the app at a production host, database, or credential when a configuration variable is unset. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: no default for environment-selecting variables; fail fast naming the variable, per DX-007. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-005 — A committed real `.env` file.** Banned: committing a `.env` (or equivalent) containing real values, or leaving it out of `.gitignore`. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Instead: commit `.env.example` with placeholders only and gitignore the real file, per DX-005 and DX-006. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-001 — Fresh-clone bootstrap test.** Verifies: DX-001, DX-008, DX-010. Check (automated): in a clean container or VM, `git clone <repo> test-clone && cd test-clone && <bootstrap command>`, then run the test suite and the app's health check; run the bootstrap a second time and repeat. Pass: app starts, tests pass, second run changes nothing, and zero undocumented steps were needed. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-002 — Example-file secret scan.** Verifies: DX-006. Check (automated): run a secret scanner (gitleaks or equivalent) over the tree, plus `git grep -nE "sk_live|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY" -- .env.example "*.example" "*.sample"` must return nothing. Pass: zero hits and every example value is an obvious placeholder. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-003 — Pin singularity and CI parity check.** Verifies: DX-002, DX-003, DX-009, DX-012. Check (automated): the pin file exists; `grep -rniE "latest" README.md docs/ <setup files>` returns no install instruction using it; CI configuration references the pin file and frozen install mode rather than naming its own tool versions. Pass: one pin file, referenced by CI, no floating versions anywhere. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-004 — Environment-variable coverage check.** Verifies: DX-005. Check (automated): extract variable names read by the code (e.g. `grep -rhoE "process\.env\.[A-Z_]+|os\.environ\[\"[A-Z_]+\"\]" src/`), extract keys from `.env.example`, and diff. Pass: zero variables missing from `.env.example`, and every entry has a purpose note. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-005 — Fail-fast startup check.** Verifies: DX-007, DX-011. Check (automated): start the app with one required variable unset, then with it set to a malformed value. Pass: both runs exit non-zero with an error naming the variable; no run silently connects to a default environment. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- One command from clone to running — a second manual step is a defect.
- Versions live in one pin file; docs reference it, never restate it.
- Examples hold placeholders; real secrets live nowhere in git.
- Missing config fails fast and names the variable — never defaults to prod.
- If it only works on your machine, the gate has failed, not the machine.

## Checklist

- [ ] One bootstrap command reaches a running app with tests green from a clean clone (DX-001, G-DX-001).
- [ ] Every tool version pinned exactly once in one committed pin file; no `latest` anywhere (DX-002, DX-003, G-DX-003).
- [ ] Lockfile committed; installs run frozen/CI mode locally and in CI (DX-004).
- [ ] `.env.example` lists every variable the code reads, with placeholder value and purpose note (DX-005, G-DX-004).
- [ ] Secret scan over examples and tree returns zero real credentials (DX-006, G-DX-002).
- [ ] App fails fast, naming any missing or malformed required variable (DX-007, G-DX-005).
- [ ] Bootstrap run twice in the clean test with no change on the second run (DX-008, G-DX-001).
- [ ] CI installs from the same pin file and lockfile as a laptop (DX-009, G-DX-003).
- [ ] Backing services declared in devcontainer/compose and started by the bootstrap (DX-010).

<!-- generated from skills/developer-experience/legacy-migration/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# legacy-migration

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://kindatechnical.com/software-engineering/large-scale-change-strangler-branch-abstraction.html ; https://microservices.io/post/refactoring/2023/06/21/strangler-fig-application-pattern-incremental-modernization-to-services.md.html ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html
- **Depends on:** tech-debt
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a working legacy system, module, or data shape must be replaced — a framework swap, a service extraction, a store or API migration — and the old behavior must keep serving users while the new one is built.
- **Do NOT use when:** the change preserves behavior inside one implementation with no old/new coexistence (use refactoring), the code is being deleted with no replacement (just delete it, with a decision-log entry), or the "legacy" system has no users yet (rewrite freely; there is nothing to migrate).

## Rules

1. **DX-121 — The plan is slices, seams, and rollbacks.** Every migration plan names its slices (one capability at a time), the seam for each slice (routing facade, abstraction layer, or expand–migrate–contract for data/API shapes), and the rollback for each step. A plan whose migration is one big step is rejected before work starts.
2. **DX-122 — Characterization tests pin behavior before anything moves.** Before a slice is touched, tests are written against the legacy implementation recording what it actually does today — including its quirks and error behavior — on production-shaped cases. The replacement is built to pass these tests, not to match a spec written from memory.
3. **DX-123 — The seam goes in first.** The facade, router, or abstraction layer is introduced and deployed with all traffic still flowing to the legacy implementation before any new implementation exists. A seam that only appears together with the new code cannot be rolled back independently and is not a seam.
4. **DX-124 — Legacy stays deployable and is the fallback.** The legacy implementation remains buildable, deployable, and monitored for the whole coexistence period. It is never edited into a half-migrated state, and no migration step may leave the project with only the new path working.
5. **DX-125 — Parallel run with compared outputs before cutover.** Before a slice's traffic flips, the new implementation runs against the same recorded production-shaped inputs as the legacy one (shadow calls, replayed requests, or dual execution) and the outputs are diffed. Every diff is either fixed or recorded as an intended behavior change with a decider named. Cutover on untested equivalence is a guess.
6. **DX-126 — Cutover is per slice and reversible in one change.** Traffic flips slice by slice through the routing seam (route rule or toggle), never all slices at once. Flipping back to legacy is a single configuration change, rehearsed in staging before the first production flip.
7. **DX-127 — Data migration is rehearsed and reversible, or its point of no return is explicit.** Every data move is first run against a copy of production-shaped data with row counts and checksums compared. The migration is reversible until a stated point of no return; a verified backup is taken at that point, and the point is named in the plan before the rehearsal, not discovered during it.
8. **DX-128 — No new features on scheduled legacy paths.** Once a slice is scheduled for migration, its legacy implementation receives fixes only. A feature that must land before the slice migrates is built in the new implementation, or the schedule is formally changed — building it in legacy "just this once" moves the target forever.
9. **DX-129 — Coexistence has an end date.** The plan states the date or release by which coexistence ends and the legacy path is eliminated. "Both systems for now" with no end date is not a stage of the plan; it is how migrations fail.
10. **DX-130 — Elimination is a separate, later step.** The legacy path is deleted only after its replacement has carried real production traffic for the soak period named in the plan, as its own reviewed change — never in the same change as the cutover, and never on cutover day.
11. **DX-131 — Shape changes use Parallel Change.** A breaking data or API shape change goes expand (new shape added alongside old, both written) → migrate (readers and writers moved, old shape still valid) → contract (old shape removed). No step breaks a reader that has not yet migrated.
12. **DX-132 — Migration state is recorded as it changes.** Each slice's stage (seamed, built, parallel-running, cut over, eliminated) and its current routing are recorded in the migration plan and progress.md at the moment they change. The routing table in production and the plan's stated stage must agree; disagreement is a defect found by G-DX-062, not a documentation nit.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-061 — Big-bang cutover.** Banned: freezing the legacy system, rewriting it wholesale, and switching everything over in one release. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: slice the migration behind a routing seam and flip one capability at a time (DX-121, DX-123, DX-126). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-062 — Legacy deleted at cutover.** Banned: removing, undeploying, or letting the legacy implementation rot in the same change that flips traffic to its replacement, leaving dead references and no fallback. Defeats: DET-CODE-002. Instead: keep legacy deployable through the soak period and delete it in a separate elimination step (DX-124, DX-130). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-063 — New features built into a scheduled legacy path.** Banned: implementing new behavior in a legacy implementation whose slice is already scheduled, so the feature exists only in code about to be replaced and must be built twice. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Instead: build it in the new implementation, or formally reschedule the slice (DX-128). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-064 — Migration with no characterization tests.** Banned: replacing a legacy path whose current behavior is pinned by no tests, so "equivalent" is asserted from reading the code or from the original spec. Defeats: DET-CODE-013. Instead: write characterization tests against the running legacy behavior first and build the replacement to pass them (DX-122). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-065 — Legacy kept as commented-out code after elimination.** Banned: leaving the removed implementation commented out, copied into a `legacy/` folder inside the shipped code, or otherwise retained in the working tree "just in case" after the eliminate step. Defeats: DET-CODE-010. Instead: delete it — version control is the archive — and record the elimination in the plan (DX-130, DX-132). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-061 — Parity suite on both implementations (automated).** Verifies: DX-122, DX-125. Check: run the slice's characterization/parity suite twice, once per implementation — `IMPL=legacy npm run test:parity -- <slice>` and `IMPL=new npm run test:parity -- <slice>` (or the project's equivalent recorded in the plan) — over the recorded production-shaped case set. Pass: exit 0 on both runs, and every output diff between the two runs is either zero or listed in the plan as an intended change with a named decider. Fail: block cutover for that slice. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-062 — Route audit (automated).** Verifies: DX-126, DX-132. Check: dump the facade/router's effective routing table and diff it against the migration plan's stated current stage: every route the plan marks "cut over" points at the new implementation, every other route at legacy, with no unlisted routes. Pass: empty diff. Fail: block shipment; reconcile the table or the plan before proceeding. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-063 — Rollback drill (automated/staging).** Verifies: DX-124, DX-126. Check: in staging, flip the slice's routing back to legacy using only the documented single configuration change, then run the primary-flow smoke tests against the legacy path. Pass: smoke tests green on legacy with no code change and no redeploy of the new implementation. Fail: block the production cutover — a rollback that has never been executed is assumed not to exist. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-064 — Post-elimination dead-reference sweep (automated).** Verifies: DX-130. Check: after an eliminate step, `grep -rn '<removed module/endpoint name>' --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=node_modules .` over source, config, and routing, plus a full build and test run. Pass: no references outside the migration plan and changelog; build and tests green. Fail: block shipment until references are removed or the elimination is reverted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-065 — Plan completeness review (manual).** Verifies: DX-121, DX-127, DX-129. Check: before the first slice is built, read the migration plan and confirm every slice names its seam, its rollback, its data point-of-no-return and backup (or "no data change"), and that the plan carries a coexistence end date. Pass: all fields present for all slices. Fail: block the start of migration work; a plan missing a rollback or an end date is not yet a plan. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Slice it behind a seam, or do not start.
- Pin the behavior before you move it — tests first, replacement second.
- Legacy is the fallback until the replacement has carried real traffic.
- Cutover is a routing flip; rollback is the same flip, backwards, already drilled.
- Coexistence without an end date is the failure mode, not a stage.

## Checklist

- [ ] The plan names every slice, its seam, and its rollback; no single-step plan (DX-121, G-DX-065).
- [ ] Characterization tests pass against the legacy implementation before the replacement is built (DX-122).
- [ ] The seam is deployed with all traffic still on legacy before new code lands behind it (DX-123).
- [ ] Parity suite passes on both implementations; every diff is fixed or recorded as intended (DX-125, G-DX-061).
- [ ] The rollback flip has been drilled in staging for this slice (DX-126, G-DX-063).
- [ ] Data moves are rehearsed on a copy; the point of no return and its backup are named (DX-127).
- [ ] No new features were added to scheduled legacy paths during this work (DX-128).
- [ ] The plan's coexistence end date stands, slice stages are recorded, and elimination is scheduled as its own later change (DX-129, DX-130, DX-132).

# monorepo-tooling

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Turborepo concepts and pipeline practice — https://www.devtoolsguide.com/turborepo-monorepo-guide/ ; mise dev tools (task/tool layer at repo root) — https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/
- **Depends on:** dev-environment, dependency-management
- **Feeds into:** versioning, ci-cd

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project has two or more deployables (web app plus API, worker, or second app) or a package genuinely shared by more than one of them, and the operator wants shared code and atomic cross-package changes in one repository.
- **Do NOT use when:** the project is a single app with no shared package — a plain single-package repo (or separate repos per deployable) is the honest default. Do not scaffold a monorepo for a landing page, and do not use this skill to split one app into packages that only exist to look architectural.

## Rules

1. **DX-021 — Stated trigger, recorded.** A monorepo is created only when the trigger holds: 2+ deployables, or one package consumed by 2+ deployables. The reason is recorded in the project's stack file or an ADR before scaffolding. No trigger, no monorepo.
2. **DX-022 — One lockfile, at the root.** Exactly one lockfile exists, at the repository root, committed. CI installs from it frozen; a package-level lockfile or an install that modifies the root lockfile is a defect.
3. **DX-023 — Declared internal dependencies only.** Every internal package a package uses is declared in that package's manifest. The task graph (build/lint/test order) is derived from those declarations by the task runner — never from a hand-maintained build-order list or script sequence.
4. **DX-024 — Entry points, not reach-across.** A package imports another package only through its declared package name and public entry point (or declared export subpaths). Relative imports that cross a package boundary are forbidden.
5. **DX-025 — Acyclic, tool-enforced boundaries.** The package dependency graph has no cycles, and boundary rules (allowed dependency directions, entry-point-only imports) are enforced by lint or graph tooling in CI — not by convention or review memory.
6. **DX-026 — Every task declares outputs.** Each build/test task in the pipeline config declares its outputs. A task that cannot declare outputs is marked uncacheable in the config with the reason written next to it.
7. **DX-027 — Cache keys cover all inputs.** Cache keys include the lockfile hash and every environment variable the task reads. A cache hit after any input changed is a correctness bug to be fixed in the key, never a speedup to be celebrated.
8. **DX-028 — Shared configs live in config packages.** TypeScript, lint, and test-preset configs live in internal config packages and are extended or referenced by each package. Config files are never copy-pasted per package.
9. **DX-029 — Root scripts are the only entry points.** `build`, `lint`, `test`, and `dev` run from the root and fan out through the task graph. Documentation names only root scripts; per-package scripts are implementation detail.
10. **DX-030 — One versioning model, chosen up front.** The repo states its model before the first release: independent per-package versioning (Changesets-style) or one fixed version for the whole repo. The two are never mixed by accident; internal dependency ranges follow the chosen model.
11. **DX-031 — Affected-only CI for changes.** Pull-request CI builds and tests only the changed packages and their dependents (affected/filter run). A change to a shared package automatically pulls every dependent into the run. The full pipeline runs on merge to the main branch.
12. **DX-032 — Deliberate internal ranges.** Internal dependencies use the workspace protocol (or the ecosystem equivalent) so local packages link locally. No internal or external dependency is declared with `*` or `latest`.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-011 — Reach-across imports.** Banned: importing another package's source by relative path (`../../api/src/db/client`) instead of its declared entry point. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: declare `@repo/api` in the web package's manifest and import the exported entry point. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-012 — Copy-pasted shared configs.** Banned: duplicating `tsconfig`, ESLint, or test-preset files into every package and editing the copies separately. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: one internal config package (e.g. `@repo/tsconfig`) that every package extends. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-013 — Undeclared internal dependency.** Banned: importing an internal package that is not declared in the importing package's manifest, relying on hoisting to make it resolve. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: declare every internal import in the manifest so the graph edge exists. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-014 — Wildcard and latest ranges.** Banned: `*` or `latest` as a version range for any dependency, internal or external. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: workspace protocol for internal packages and the project's deliberate range policy for external ones, resolved by the single root lockfile. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-015 — Monorepo without a trigger.** Banned: scaffolding workspaces, a task runner, and shared packages for a single deployable with no shared package. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Instead: a plain single-package repo; adopt this skill when a second deployable or a genuinely shared package appears. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-011 — Double-run cache verification.** Verifies: DX-026, DX-027. Check: automated — from a clean checkout, run the full root pipeline twice (`turbo run build test` or the Nx equivalent); hash all declared outputs after each run and `diff` the two hash lists. Pass: the second run reports cache hits for every unchanged package and the outputs are byte-identical. Fail: block shipment; fix the task's declared outputs or cache inputs. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-012 — Affected-only rebuild test.** Verifies: DX-023, DX-031. Check: automated — in a scratch clone, touch one file in a leaf package and run the CI affected command (e.g. `turbo run build --filter=...HEAD^` or `nx affected`); then touch one file in a shared package and repeat. Pass: the first run builds only the leaf and its dependents, and the second run includes every dependent of the shared package. Fail: block shipment; the graph is missing a declared edge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-013 — Boundary and cycle check.** Verifies: DX-024, DX-025. Check: automated — run the boundary lint/graph check in CI (e.g. the task runner's graph validation plus `grep -rn "from '\.\./" packages/*/src apps/*/src` excluding same-package relative imports), and a cycle detector over the package graph. Pass: zero cross-boundary relative imports and zero cycles. Fail: block the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-014 — Single-lockfile frozen install.** Verifies: DX-022, DX-032. Check: automated — `find . -name "*lock*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"` (ecosystem equivalent) returns exactly one lockfile at the root; then a frozen install (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` or equivalent) succeeds and `git status` shows the lockfile unmodified. Pass: one lockfile, frozen install clean. Fail: block the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- No trigger, no monorepo.
- One repo, one lockfile, one version policy.
- If it is imported, it is declared; the graph comes from the manifests.
- Entry points only — never reach across a boundary.
- A cache hit on changed inputs is a bug, not a speedup.

## Checklist

- [ ] The monorepo trigger is recorded and still holds (DX-021).
- [ ] Exactly one lockfile, at the root, and the frozen install leaves it untouched (G-DX-014).
- [ ] Every internal import is declared in the importing package's manifest (DX-023).
- [ ] Zero cross-boundary relative imports and zero package cycles (G-DX-013).
- [ ] Every task declares outputs, or is marked uncacheable with a reason (DX-026).
- [ ] Double-run check passed: cache hits with byte-identical outputs (G-DX-011).
- [ ] Affected-only run rebuilds a shared package's dependents (G-DX-012).
- [ ] Shared configs come from config packages; no copy-pasted config files (DX-028).
- [ ] The versioning model is stated and internal ranges follow it (DX-030, DX-032).

# project-takeover

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks ; https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-secret-scanning ; https://12factor.net/config ; https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/
- **Depends on:** dev-environment (the local run in DX-185 follows its bootstrap and pin discipline), tech-debt (the register that receives every non-stabilization finding under DX-190)
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, legacy-migration, dependency-management

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a team or agent inherits an existing project it did not build — a handover from a departing developer, a contractor delivery, an acquired or rescued codebase, an abandoned repo being revived — and must take responsibility for it. This skill is the entry protocol: inventory what exists, get it running locally, audit it, build the risk map, and stabilize it, in that order, before any other work begins.
- **Do NOT use when:** the project is your own ongoing work (no takeover is occurring), the system is being replaced rather than inherited (once takeover completes and the system is stable, use legacy-migration for the replacement), the task is a one-off code review of code you will not own (a review produces findings; a takeover produces an owned, running, risk-mapped system), or the inherited system is a throwaway prototype with no users, no production data, and no live integrations (archive it or rewrite freely; there is nothing to secure).
- **Boundary with neighbors:** this skill is the BEFORE phase. It ends at a stabilized, understood system and a signed-off takeover report. Everything the audit finds that is not stabilization is handed off, not done here: known shortcuts go to the tech-debt register (tech-debt), behavior-preserving cleanup waits for refactoring, system replacement waits for legacy-migration, and version currency waits for dependency-management. Where those skills define a discipline this skill needs — register fields, characterization tests, frozen installs — this skill references them instead of restating them. The overlap with prototype-hardening is decided by what the inherited system carries: a rough inherited prototype with live users, production data, or live integrations comes through takeover first, and hardening is scheduled as post-exit work under DX-190; a rough inherited prototype with none of those goes straight to prototype-hardening, and takeover never runs.

## Rules

1. **DX-181 — Takeover mode is declared and freezes the scope of work.** The takeover starts with a dated declaration in progress.md naming the project, the source it was inherited from, and the starting commit or snapshot (DX-183). From that moment until the exit gate (G-DX-095) passes, the only permitted work is inventory, local run, audit, risk mapping, and stabilization under DX-191. No feature work, no cleanup, no upgrades — however small, however obviously needed — are performed in takeover mode.
2. **DX-182 — Inventory before opinion.** Before any judgment about the project's quality or future is recorded, a takeover inventory exists listing: every repository and its branches; every deployable service and where it runs; every data store and its owner; every scheduled job, webhook, and external integration; every environment (dev, staging, production, and any per-machine variants); and every document, dashboard, and runbook that came with the handover. Each item is marked `verified` (the inheritor has seen it working or inspected it directly), `claimed` (asserted by the predecessor or the docs, not yet checked), or `unknown` (known to exist, not yet located). An item may not be marked `verified` on someone else's word — that is DX-186.
3. **DX-183 — The inherited state is preserved before it is touched.** The first action on the code is preservation, not exploration-by-edit: record the starting commit hash and `git status` output, preserve any uncommitted changes exactly as found (stash copy, patch file, or a snapshot branch — never discard, clean, or "tidy" them), and note the state of any non-versioned material that came with the handover (loose config files, database dumps, exported keys). If the inherited material has no version control, initializing a repository over it — committing the state exactly as received — is the first stabilization change and precedes all others.
4. **DX-184 — Access and ownership are mapped, including what is missing.** The inventory names, for each external thing the project depends on — domain registrar and DNS, cloud/hosting account, CI provider, package and container registries, app stores, payment and email providers, error-tracking and analytics accounts — who holds administrative access today: the inheritor, the predecessor personally, a company account, or nobody knows. Anything held only by the predecessor, or by nobody identifiable, is a top-section risk-map entry (DX-190) from the day it is discovered, not a surprise saved for later. Credentials are transferred through the project's secret store, never through chat, email, or committed files.
5. **DX-185 — It runs locally from a clean clone, from the repo's own instructions.** The inheritor clones the project fresh and brings it up following only what the repository itself documents, under dev-environment's bootstrap and pin discipline. Every step that is missing, wrong, or known only to the predecessor is recorded as a takeover finding with the exact step that had to be discovered. "It ran on the predecessor's machine" is not a run; the takeover run happens on a machine or container with none of the predecessor's local state. Setup defects found here are findings — repairing the bootstrap is stabilization (DX-191), redesigning the environment is not.
6. **DX-186 — Every handover claim is re-verified or stays `claimed`.** Statements from the predecessor, the README, or the delivery note — "tests pass," "deployed from main," "backups are on," "that service is unused," "the cron was disabled" — are claims, not facts. Each material claim is either reproduced by the inheritor (run, read, or queried directly) and upgraded to `verified` in the inventory, or it remains `claimed` and appears in the risk map with its potential impact if false. The takeover report — inventory, baseline, audit, and risk map, signed off at G-DX-095 — never restates a `claimed` item in the language of fact.
7. **DX-187 — The as-found baseline is recorded before anything changes.** Once the project runs locally (DX-185), the inheritor records its state exactly as inherited: build result, full test-suite result (pass/fail counts as found, not as hoped), lint/type-check result where configured, and a smoke pass over the primary user flows. Pre-existing failures are findings with their output preserved; they are not fixed during baselining, and the baseline is never re-recorded after a fix to make the inheritance look healthier. Every later change — in takeover and after — is judged against this baseline.
8. **DX-188 — A security audit precedes any change to the running system.** Before the first stabilization change, the audit covers at minimum: a secret scan over the working tree and the full version-control history (gitleaks or equivalent); a dependency vulnerability audit with findings routed per dependency-management (DX-071 there) to D7 dependency-safety; the authentication and authorization surface (who can log in, what roles exist, whether any test, default, or predecessor personal accounts are live); exposed debug, admin, or default surfaces in production configuration; and where production credentials and personal accounts are still active. A live secret found anywhere — tree, history, CI logs, a handover document — is treated as compromised: rotation is stabilization and happens under DX-191, and the finding records that rotation, not deletion of the file, is what closes it.
9. **DX-189 — The detection sweep is run and its hits are recorded by ID.** The inherited codebase and its infrastructure are swept with the repo's detection parameters — skills/detection/code/PARAMETERS.md and skills/detection/infra/PARAMETERS.md at minimum — and every hit is entered in the audit by its DET ID, with the file or configuration that triggered it. Hits are findings, not a work list: only hits that meet the stabilization bar (DX-191) are acted on during takeover; the rest transfer to the risk map and the tech-debt register under DX-190. A sweep that was "done mentally" while reading code does not count — the recorded hit list is the evidence it happened.
10. **DX-190 — Every finding gets a risk-map disposition.** The risk map is a single table in the takeover report: one row per audit, inventory, baseline, and access finding, each with likelihood, impact, a named owner, and exactly one disposition — `stabilize-now` (meets DX-191), `register` (transferred to the tech-debt register under tech-debt's field rules, with the register ID recorded here), `schedule` (named follow-on work under refactoring, legacy-migration, or dependency-management, with a trigger or date), or `accept` (a named decider consciously accepts the risk, recorded as such). A finding with no disposition is an unfinished takeover, and the highest-impact rows are summarized at the top of the report, not buried in the table.
11. **DX-191 — Stabilization is minimal, separable, and the only change permitted.** A change qualifies as stabilization only if it makes the inherited system safe or runnable without changing its intended behavior: rotating a compromised secret, restoring a broken build or a missing pin so the as-found code runs, enabling or verifying a backup for production data, closing an exposed debug/admin surface, or revoking a departed predecessor's live access. Each stabilization change is its own commit or pull request, labeled as takeover stabilization, and judged against the DX-187 baseline. Anything that improves structure, updates a version, or adds behavior fails this test by definition and waits for takeover exit — "while I'm in here" is precisely the failure this rule exists to prevent.
12. **DX-192 — Production data and backups are verified, never assumed.** The inventory names every production data store, where its backups live, how often they run, and when a restore was last actually performed. During takeover the inheritor performs or witnesses a restore of the most critical store into a non-production environment; a backup that has never been restore-tested is recorded as `claimed`, and the risk map carries the honest entry "no verified recovery path" until a restore succeeds. The first local run and all takeover experimentation use copies, fixtures, or anonymized data — never live production data on a laptop (see BAN-DX-094).

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-091 — Work before the freeze lifts.** Banned: any feature, cleanup, refactoring, or dependency/framework upgrade change made between the takeover declaration and the exit gate, alone or mixed into a stabilization change. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: record the bug, the upgrade, and the rename as risk-map findings with dispositions (DX-190); only DX-191 stabilization ships during takeover, each change separate. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-092 — Handover claims accepted as verified.** Banned: marking any inventory item `verified`, or reporting the project healthy, on the predecessor's statement, the README, or a delivery note, without the inheritor reproducing it. Defeats: DET-CRWL-004. Instead: reproduce each material claim or leave it `claimed` and risk-mapped, under DX-186 and DX-192. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-093 — Inherited secrets left live or passed around in the clear.** Banned: finding a real secret in the tree, history, or handover material and leaving it in place "until later," or transferring predecessor credentials through chat, email, or a committed file. Defeats: DET-INF-005. Instead: treat it as compromised, rotate it as stabilization (DX-188, DX-191), transfer all credentials through the secret store (DX-184), and record the rotation as the closure. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-094 — First run pointed at production.** Banned: running the inherited system locally or in a test environment while it is configured with production databases, queues, payment providers, email/SMS senders, or third-party webhooks. Defeats: DET-INF-003. Instead: run against copies, fixtures, or sandbox credentials only (DX-192); an environment whose production separation cannot be established is itself a `stabilize-now` finding. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-095 — Unknown things deleted as "dead."** Banned: deleting, disabling, or decommissioning any inherited file, service, scheduled job, account, DNS record, or data store during takeover because it looks unused, unreferenced, or undocumented. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names the deletion of a live-but-unrecognized component; governed by DX-182 and DX-190. Instead: an unrecognized item is inventoried as `unknown` (DX-182) and risk-mapped; removal, if ever, is a post-takeover change made with evidence of non-use gathered while the system runs observed. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-091 — Inventory completeness gate (manual + automated).** Verifies: DX-182, DX-184. Check: diff the inventory against independent sources of truth — the cloud/hosting account's resource list, DNS records for the project's domains, the CI provider's project list, and `git branch -a` plus top-level tree of every repository — and confirm every discovered resource appears in the inventory and every inventory item carries `verified` / `claimed` / `unknown` and, for external services, an access holder (DX-184). Pass: zero unlisted resources and zero unmarked items. Fail: block; takeover remains in inventory phase. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-092 — Clean-clone run and baseline gate (automated).** Verifies: DX-185, DX-187. Check: in a clean container or VM, clone the repository, follow only the repo's documented setup, start the app, run the full test suite and the primary-flow smoke pass, and save the outputs as the baseline record. Pass: the app runs, the baseline record exists with build, test counts, and smoke results exactly as found, and every undocumented step needed is logged as a finding. Fail: block; a project that cannot be run by its inheritor has not been taken over — the blocker itself becomes the top stabilization item. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-093 — Security and detection sweep gate (automated).** Verifies: DX-188, DX-189. Check: run the secret scanner over tree and history (`gitleaks detect --log-opts="--all"` or equivalent), the ecosystem dependency audit, and the DET sweep checklists for code and infra; confirm the audit document lists every hit by DET ID or scanner finding, and that every live-secret hit shows a rotation record. Pass: all three sweeps run, hits recorded, zero unrotated live secrets. Fail: block; no stabilization change to the running system precedes this gate. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-094 — Risk-map disposition gate (automated + manual).** Verifies: DX-190. Check: parse the risk-map table: every row has likelihood, impact, owner, and one of the four dispositions; every `register` row names a tech-debt register ID that exists in `docs/tech-debt.md`; every `accept` row names a decider; every `stabilize-now` row links its stabilization change. Pass: zero undispositioned findings. Fail: block exit; a finding without a disposition is assigned one before takeover closes. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-095 — Freeze and exit gate (automated + manual).** Verifies: DX-181, DX-191, DX-192. Check: audit every commit since the takeover declaration (`git log --oneline <start-commit>..HEAD` and the change list for non-git material) — each change is labeled stabilization and maps to a `stabilize-now` risk-map row; confirm the critical-store restore test (DX-192) is recorded as performed or the "no verified recovery path" risk stands at the top of the report with a named owner; a named owner signs the takeover report (inventory, baseline, audit, risk map) in progress.md. Pass: no non-stabilization change in the range, restore status honestly recorded, report signed. Fail: block; takeover mode continues and the offending change is reverted or formally reclassified as the start of post-takeover work with the takeover declared failed and restarted. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Understand and secure first — no feature work, no cleanup, no upgrades until the protocol completes.
- Inventory before opinion; every item is verified, claimed, or unknown — and only reproduction earns "verified."
- Preserve the as-found state, record the as-found baseline; later arguments are settled by those two records.
- A found live secret is a compromised secret: rotation is the closure, not deleting the file.
- Every finding leaves takeover with a disposition and an owner — stabilize, register, schedule, or a named acceptance.

## Checklist

- [ ] Takeover declared in progress.md with source and starting commit/snapshot; scope frozen (DX-181, DX-183).
- [ ] Inventory complete against independent sources; every item marked verified/claimed/unknown (DX-182, G-DX-091).
- [ ] Access and ownership map written, including everything held only by the predecessor or by nobody (DX-184).
- [ ] Project runs from a clean clone using only repo instructions; every undocumented step logged as a finding (DX-185, G-DX-092).
- [ ] As-found baseline (build, test counts, smoke results) recorded before any change (DX-187).
- [ ] Security audit and DET sweep done; hits recorded by ID; every live secret rotated (DX-188, DX-189, G-DX-093).
- [ ] Critical data store restore-tested, or "no verified recovery path" stands as a top risk (DX-192).
- [ ] Risk map complete: every finding has likelihood, impact, owner, and one disposition (DX-190, G-DX-094).
- [ ] Every change since the declaration is a separate, labeled stabilization change — nothing else (DX-191, G-DX-095).
- [ ] Takeover report signed by a named owner; post-takeover work handed to tech-debt, refactoring, legacy-migration, or dependency-management, not started here (DX-190, G-DX-095).
