# prototype-hardening

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Authentication Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html ; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Input Validation Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html ; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html ; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Secrets Management Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html ; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, Error Handling Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html ; OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) — https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/
- **Depends on:** placeholder-scan (its verdict is an input, not the repair), tech-debt (shortcuts deliberately kept during hardening are registered there)
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, security-testing, e2e-testing, versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a rough MVP, demo, hackathon build, no-code export, or AI-generated prototype — software that was built to be shown, not to be trusted — is being promoted to real users, real data, or real money, and needs one deliberate conversion pass: replacing simulated behavior with real behavior, closing the security holes prototypes ship with, adding the error handling and data-integrity guarantees the demo never needed, and proving the result with tests. The output is a hardening ledger and a production / not-production verdict, not a prettier codebase.
- **Do NOT use when:** the code is already production-grade and only its internal structure needs improving with behavior unchanged — that is refactoring (DX-101–DX-120), and hardening rules must not be used to smuggle behavior changes into a refactoring change. Do NOT use when a working legacy system with live users is being replaced in slices while the old system keeps serving — that is legacy-migration (DX-121–DX-140); a prototype has no incumbent behavior worth preserving, which is exactly why it can be hardened in place instead of migrated. Do NOT use when the task is only to find placeholder or fake content — that verdict belongs to placeholder-scan (QA-281–QA-292), which detects; this skill repairs what it finds and must not re-define its fingerprints or probes. Do NOT use to catalogue known shortcuts without fixing them — that register work is tech-debt (DX-081–DX-100). Do NOT use when the honest answer is a rewrite: if the prototype's data model or core flow is wrong, say so and stop; hardening a wrong foundation produces a hardened wrong product. Do NOT use as the entry point for an inherited prototype that carries live obligations you have not yet taken ownership of: if the prototype came from someone else and has live users, production data, or live integrations, run project-takeover first (inventory, access map, as-found baseline, secret rotation) and harden only after its exit gate; an inherited prototype with none of those is hardened directly, with this skill's ledger as its entry record.

## Rules

1. **DX-161 — Inventory before touching code.** Before any fix, produce the hardening ledger: every route, screen, endpoint, job, and integration in the prototype, each classified as REAL (works end to end against the real store), SIMULATED (stub, fixture, in-memory, or client-only), or ABSENT (implied by the UI but not implemented). The ledger is built by exercising the running prototype — clicking, submitting, reloading, signing in with a wrong password — not by reading the code and believing its comments. No hardening work starts on an un-inventoried area.
2. **DX-162 — The prototype is untrusted input.** Every claim the prototype makes about itself — "login works," "payments are wired," "data is saved" — is treated as false until re-proven against the production-shaped stack. A feature is REAL only when its effect survives a reload, a re-login, and a server restart, and is visible in the underlying store, not only in the UI.
3. **DX-163 — Scope is the conversion, nothing else.** Hardening changes how trustworthy existing behavior is, not what the product does. New features, redesigns, and stack swaps discovered mid-pass are recorded as follow-ups, not built. The one exception: a simulated core function (DX-161) is implemented for real or removed from the shipped surface — leaving it simulated is not a scope option.
4. **DX-164 — Auth is real, server-side, and complete.** Authentication is implemented or replaced with a real mechanism: credentials are verified server-side against stored, properly hashed passwords (or a managed identity provider), sessions are issued and invalidated server-side, and password reset actually changes the credential and invalidates old sessions. The session cookie is HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite, the session identifier is rotated at login and at every privilege change so a pre-login identifier can never be fixated, and the credential endpoints are rate-limited with lockout or progressive delay so the login form is not a guessing oracle (session mechanics per `session-security`, D7; throttling per `rate-limiting`, D4 — this skill requires both, it does not restate them). Client-side flags, stored "logged in" booleans, and any-password acceptance are deleted, not layered over. Authorization is checked server-side on every privileged request, independent of what the UI hides (see DET-FAKE-021).
5. **DX-165 — No secret ships in code, history, or bundle.** Every credential, API key, token, and connection string found in source, configuration defaults, committed history, or the client bundle is treated as compromised: it is rotated, moved to the environment or a secrets store, and the old value is revoked — moving it to an environment variable without rotating it does not close the finding. The hardened tree and the built client bundle are both scanned; a key that only left the source but still ships in the bundle is still shipped.
6. **DX-166 — Every boundary validates input.** Every value crossing a trust boundary — form fields, query and path parameters, headers, file uploads, webhook and API payloads — is validated server-side for type, range, length, and allowed values, and rejected with a safe error when it fails. Client-side validation may exist for UX but never counts as the control. Queries are parameterized, output in templates is escaped by the framework default, and file uploads are checked for type and size and stored outside executable paths.
7. **DX-167 — Errors are handled, logged, and safe to show.** No I/O boundary — database, network, filesystem, external API, payment provider — runs without an error path. Each failure is logged server-side with enough context to diagnose it (operation, correlation/request identifier, underlying error), and the user sees a generic message that reveals no stack traces, query text, internal paths, or provider internals. Empty catch blocks, catch-and-continue, and success responses returned on failure are removed wherever found.
8. **DX-168 — Data integrity is enforced by the store, not by hope.** The hardened schema carries the constraints the prototype skipped: primary and foreign keys, uniqueness where the domain requires it (account email, idempotency keys, external references), NOT NULL on required fields, and transactions around every multi-write operation so a failure mid-operation leaves no partial state. Retried or double-submitted writes — form resubmits, webhook redeliveries, client retries — are made idempotent where a duplicate would charge, create, or send twice.
9. **DX-169 — Fake and placeholder content is removed, not relabeled.** Seed users, fixture catalogs, canned search/AI responses, staged notifications, lorem ipsum, placeholder contacts, and demo numbers found by the inventory (DX-161) or by placeholder-scan are deleted from production code paths and production seed state. What replaces them is real data flow plus honest empty states: a new account sees an empty workspace, not staged content. A demo mode that must survive is isolated behind an explicit, labeled, non-production configuration and can never be enabled by the production environment.
10. **DX-170 — The critical paths get real tests.** Automated tests are added for, at minimum: authentication (correct password accepted, wrong password rejected, reset invalidates the old credential), authorization (a low-privilege account replaying a privileged request is rejected server-side), each core write flow (the write persists and survives reload), each payment or irreversible action if one exists (including its failure and duplicate-submission cases), and the error paths added under DX-167. A test that cannot fail — no assertion, assertion on a mock's own return value, or a stubbed subject — does not count toward this rule.
11. **DX-171 — Configuration is explicit and environments are separated.** All environment-specific values come from configuration, never from hardcoded URLs, keys, or per-machine files in code. Development, staging, and production use separate credentials and separate data stores; debug modes, verbose error pages, sample-data seeders, and admin or debug endpoints are disabled or absent in the production configuration, and the production configuration is the one the gates below run against.
12. **DX-172 — Dependencies are real, pinned, and patched.** Every import resolves to a package declared in the manifest; hallucinated or undeclared packages are removed or replaced with the real API. Versions are locked by the lockfile, the production install is reproducible from a clean checkout, and dependencies with known critical or high vulnerabilities affecting used code paths are upgraded or replaced before the verdict — the audit report is filed in the ledger, not just run and discarded.
13. **DX-173 — The prototype's shortcuts become register entries, not secrets.** Any shortcut deliberately kept at the end of the pass — a known weak spot, a deferred test, a temporary workaround — is entered in the tech-debt register under DX-081–DX-092 with its interest and repayment trigger, and named in the hardening ledger. A shortcut that exists only in the hardening agent's head or in a code comment is an undisclosed risk and blocks the verdict.
14. **DX-174 — The pass ends in a verdict, per area.** Each inventoried area is closed as HARDENED (all applicable rules met and gates passed), REMOVED (the simulated or unsafe surface was deleted), or BLOCKED (named reason, named owner, named follow-up). "Mostly done" is not a status. The product may be declared production-ready only when no core area is BLOCKED and no SIMULATED core function remains reachable in the production build.
15. **DX-175 — Rollback and recovery exist before real users arrive.** Before the hardened build takes real traffic: database migrations are rehearsed against a copy of production-shaped data and are reversible or preceded by a verified backup, a restore of that backup has been performed once, and the previous deployable build can be restored by one documented step. A hardening pass that makes the prototype safer to run but impossible to recover has not finished.
16. **DX-176 — Observability is the minimum, not the roadmap.** The hardened build emits structured server-side logs that persist beyond the process, exposes a health check that reflects its real dependencies (store reachable, not merely process alive), and surfaces server errors somewhere a named human or alert actually sees them. Console output on a developer's terminal is not observability.
17. **DX-177 — Proven behavior is pinned before it is changed.** Before any component classified REAL in the ledger (DX-161) is modified, its observable behavior — the flows the prototype actually proved — is pinned by characterization tests that pass against the unmodified component (the method is owned by `test-strategy`, D8; this skill makes pinning a precondition, it does not restate the technique). During hardening the pins run on every change: a failing pin means the change altered proven behavior, which is either a defect to fix or a deliberate behavior change recorded as a requirements change — never a test quietly edited to match the new behavior. Components classified SIMULATED or ABSENT have nothing to pin; their behavior is specified by DX-170's tests instead.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-081 — Client-only or any-password authentication.** Banned: shipping authentication that is decided in the browser, accepts any or a hardcoded password, or treats a stored "logged in" flag as a session. Defeats: DET-FAKE-001. Instead: verify credentials server-side against properly hashed stored passwords (or a managed identity provider), issue a server-side session, and reject a wrong password — proven by the wrong-password test in DX-170. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-082 — Secrets in source, history, or the client bundle.** Banned: API keys, tokens, or credentials hardcoded in code, committed to version control, shipped as configuration defaults, or embedded in the built client bundle. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Instead: rotate the exposed credential, revoke the old value, load the replacement from the environment or a secrets store at runtime, and re-scan the tree, history, and built bundle (DX-165). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-083 — Stub handlers presented as finished features.** Banned: an endpoint, handler, or function that returns a constant, an empty result, or a success response without doing the work, while the UI presents the feature as working. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Instead: implement the handler against the real store, or remove the feature from the shipped surface until it is implemented (DX-163). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-084 — Seed and fixture data shipped as real data.** Banned: demo users, fixture catalogs, canned result sets, or staged activity reachable from, imported by, or seeded into the production build as if they were real. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Instead: delete the fixtures from production code paths and seed state, ship honest empty states, and isolate any surviving demo data behind a labeled non-production configuration (DX-169). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-085 — String-built queries from user input.** Banned: constructing SQL or query strings by concatenating or interpolating unvalidated user input. Defeats: DET-CODE-017. Instead: use parameterized queries or the ORM's bound parameters for every value, with server-side validation at the boundary (DX-166). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-086 — Swallowed errors and success-on-failure.** Banned: empty exception handlers, catch blocks that only log to the browser console or do nothing, and handlers that return a success response after an underlying operation failed. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Instead: log the failure server-side with context, return a safe generic error to the user, and leave the operation's state consistent and retryable (DX-167, DX-168). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-087 — Security controls disabled to make the prototype run.** Banned: shipping with authentication or authorization checks commented out, TLS verification disabled, permissive wildcard cross-origin settings on authenticated endpoints, or framework security protections (such as CSRF or output escaping) turned off to silence an error. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: fix the underlying cause — valid certificates, a finished login, an explicit origin allow-list — and re-enable the control before the verdict (DX-164, DX-166). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-088 — Tests that assert nothing, kept to look tested.** Banned: presenting a suite as coverage of a critical path when its tests contain no meaningful assertion, assert only a mock's own behavior, or have their failing cases deleted or skipped to go green. Defeats: DET-CODE-012. Instead: write tests that exercise the real path and can fail — wrong password rejected, privileged replay refused, write persisted (DX-170) — and keep a failing test red until the code, not the test, is fixed. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-081 — Ledger completeness check.** Verifies: DX-161, DX-162, DX-174. Check: manual, against the ledger — pick three routes, one write flow, and the auth flow at random from the running production-configured build; exercise each (submit, reload, re-login, restart the server) and confirm its ledger classification (REAL / SIMULATED / ABSENT) matches the observed behavior and the underlying store. Pass: every sampled classification is accurate and every core area carries a DX-174 status. Fail: block the verdict; re-inventory the mismatched area. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-082 — Auth and authorization probe.** Verifies: DX-164. Check: automated or scripted manual probe against the production-configured build — (1) sign in with a wrong password, (2) request a protected page with no session, (3) replay a privileged request captured from an admin session using a low-privilege session, (4) complete a password reset and confirm the old credential no longer works, (5) confirm the session identifier issued at login differs from any pre-login identifier (fixation probe). Pass: all five are rejected or behave as specified, server-side. Fail: block shipment; any single success is a P0 defect. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-083 — Secret and placeholder sweep of the shipped artifact.** Verifies: DX-165, DX-169. Check: automated — run a secret scanner over the working tree, the full committed history, and the built client bundle, and run the placeholder-scan static sweep (QA-284's fingerprint set, run as gate G-QA-141) over the rendered production output; then create a fresh production account and confirm it shows empty states, not staged content. Pass: zero secret findings in tree, history, or bundle, zero placeholder findings, fresh account empty. Fail: block shipment; rotate any exposed credential under DX-165 before re-running. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-084 — Failure and integrity drill.** Verifies: DX-167, DX-168. Check: automated or scripted manual drill in staging with production configuration — (1) force each external dependency (store, provider, API) to fail once and observe the user-facing error and the server log, (2) double-submit each core write form and redeliver one webhook or retried request, (3) interrupt one multi-write operation mid-way. Pass: users see generic safe errors with no internals, every failure is logged with a correlation identifier, no duplicate charge/record/send results, and no partial state remains. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-085 — Critical-path test run.** Verifies: DX-170, DX-172, DX-177. Check: automated — from a clean checkout, install from the lockfile, build, and run the full suite in CI; confirm the DX-170 test list exists by name (auth accept/reject, reset invalidation, authorization replay, core write persistence, irreversible-action failure and duplicate cases), that the DX-177 characterization pins for every kept component's proven flows exist and were recorded green against the unmodified prototype in the ledger before hardening began, and that the dependency audit report is filed in the ledger. Pass: build and suite green with every named test and pin present and passing, and no unaddressed critical/high audit finding on a used code path. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-086 — Recovery rehearsal.** Verifies: DX-171, DX-175, DX-176. Check: manual drill in staging — restore the pre-release backup into a scratch environment and start the build against it, roll back to the previous deployable build by the one documented step, and call the health check with the data store stopped. Pass: restore and rollback both succeed, the health check reports unhealthy when its store is down, and the production configuration shows debug modes and debug/admin endpoints disabled or absent. Fail: block the production verdict until rehearsed successfully. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- A prototype's claims about itself are false until re-proven against the store.
- Inventory first: REAL, SIMULATED, or ABSENT — for every surface.
- Real auth, rotated secrets, validated input, handled errors, constrained data.
- Remove the fake; never layer the real over it.
- The pass ends in a verdict per area — "mostly done" is not one.

## Checklist

- [ ] Hardening ledger exists: every route, flow, and integration classified REAL / SIMULATED / ABSENT by exercising the running prototype (DX-161, DX-162).
- [ ] Auth is real and server-side; wrong-password, no-session, privileged-replay, and reset probes all pass (DX-164, G-DX-082).
- [ ] Every secret found in tree, history, or bundle was rotated and revoked, and the re-scan of tree, history, and bundle is clean (DX-165, G-DX-083).
- [ ] Proven flows of every kept component were pinned by characterization tests before modification, and every pin failure was resolved as a defect or a recorded behavior change (DX-177, G-DX-085).
- [ ] All boundary input is validated server-side and all queries are parameterized (DX-166).
- [ ] No swallowed errors remain on I/O boundaries; failures log server-side with context and show users a generic message (DX-167).
- [ ] Schema constraints and transactions are in place, and duplicate submission of core writes is idempotent (DX-168, G-DX-084).
- [ ] Placeholder-scan sweep of the production output is clean and a fresh account shows real empty states (DX-169, G-DX-083).
- [ ] Critical-path tests exist by name, can fail, and pass from a clean checkout in CI (DX-170, G-DX-085).
- [ ] Production configuration is separated, debug surfaces are off, and dependencies are locked with the audit report filed (DX-171, DX-172).
- [ ] Every shortcut kept is a tech-debt register entry named in the ledger (DX-173).
- [ ] Backup restore and one-step rollback were rehearsed, and the health check fails when its store is down (DX-175, DX-176, G-DX-086).
- [ ] Every area is closed HARDENED, REMOVED, or BLOCKED — no core area BLOCKED, no SIMULATED core function reachable (DX-174).

# refactoring

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://martinfowler.com/articles/workflowsOfRefactoring/fallback.html ; https://deepwiki.com/gmoral/Books/7.3-refactoring:-improving-the-design-of-existing-code
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: restructuring decisions are made from the code under change itself, read directly, with behavior pinned by the project's existing tests; no other skill's output is an input. It feeds legacy-migration and tech-debt.
- **Feeds into:** legacy-migration, tech-debt

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** code must be restructured — duplication removed, names clarified, a function decomposed, coupling reduced — to make a coming feature or fix easy, or while reading unfamiliar code (comprehension refactoring); the work changes internal structure only.
- **Do NOT use when:** observable behavior must change (that is a feature or fix change, committed separately), a whole system or module is being replaced (use legacy-migration), or the goal is measurable performance improvement (benchmarked performance work, its own change type).
- **Cross-reference:** the commented-out-code pattern banned here as BAN-DX-054 is also banned as standing debt in tech-debt (BAN-DX-042); the two entries cover the same pattern in different moments.

## Rules

1. **DX-101 — Behavior is the contract.** A refactoring leaves observable behavior identical: same outputs, API responses, persisted data, side effects, and error behavior for every input. Any change that alters observable behavior is not a refactoring — it is reclassified, renamed, and reviewed as the feature, fix, or rewrite it actually is.
2. **DX-102 — Safety net before structure.** The full relevant test suite is run and green before the first structural step. Where the area lacks tests, the first step is characterization tests that pin current behavior — including its quirks — and they land in their own preceding commit before any restructuring begins.
3. **DX-103 — Two hats, never both.** While refactoring, no features are added and no bugs are fixed; while adding features, no opportunistic restructuring is folded in. Switching hats is explicit: the refactoring commits and the behavior commits are separate, so each can be reviewed and reverted on its own.
4. **DX-104 — Small, named steps.** Each step is one named transformation from the refactoring catalog (Extract Function, Inline Variable, Change Function Declaration, Rename, Move, …), small enough that the suite runs between steps. A step too big to describe with one catalog name is split before it is committed.
5. **DX-105 — Red means stop and back up.** If the suite goes red mid-refactoring, work stops and the last step is undone or corrected; the suite is never pushed through, and the failure is never "fixed" by adjusting the code's behavior or the test. Two consecutive red steps mean the step size is too large — halve it.
6. **DX-106 — Tests are read-only during a refactoring.** No test file is added to, edited, or deleted inside a refactoring change (characterization tests under DX-102 land before it, separately). A test that appears to need changing is evidence the change alters behavior: stop and reclassify under DX-101.
7. **DX-107 — Refactor toward a named pressure.** Every refactoring change states the design pressure it answers — duplication, coupling, unclear names, runaway complexity — in its description. "Cleaner," "nicer," or "more modern" is not a pressure and does not justify a change.
8. **DX-108 — Rule of Three for abstractions.** A shared abstraction is extracted only when the same logic or shape appears for the third time. The first occurrence is written plainly; the second is duplicated deliberately and noted; the third triggers the extraction.
9. **DX-109 — The public surface does not move.** Exported symbols, API routes, and contracts are byte-identical before and after a refactoring. A change that must alter the public surface uses legacy-migration techniques (branch by abstraction, parallel change), not a refactoring commit.
10. **DX-110 — Preparatory refactoring precedes the feature.** When a feature is hard to add because of the code's shape, the order is: first make the change easy (refactoring commits, suite green), then make the easy change (feature commits). The two phases are never interleaved in one commit.
11. **DX-111 — Performance work is not refactoring.** An optimization changes a measurable quality, so it is benchmarked before and after, states its target metric, and is labeled as its own change type. It is never smuggled in under a "refactor" label, where its behavior risk would escape review.
12. **DX-112 — Replaced code is deleted in the same change.** Once an extraction or move lands, the superseded implementation is deleted — not commented out, not kept "just in case." Version control is the archive; anything worth remembering about the old shape goes to the changelog or decision log.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-051 — Tests edited to fit the refactor.** Banned: modifying, weakening, or deleting a test inside a refactoring change so the suite passes against restructured code. Defeats: DET-CODE-012. Instead: the failing test is proof of a behavior change — restore the exact behavior, or split the rounding change out as its own fix commit with its own test change (DX-101, DX-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-052 — Big-bang rewrite committed as a "refactor."** Banned: replacing a module in one unreviewable diff — hundreds of lines changed at once — under a refactoring label. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: decompose the work into named catalog steps, one commit each, suite green between steps; if the module truly needs replacement, run it as legacy-migration (DX-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-053 — Speculative abstraction for a single use.** Banned: extracting a generic framework, strategy layer, or configuration-driven engine around logic that exists exactly once, "for future flexibility." Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Instead: write the single case plainly; extract only at the third real occurrence (DX-108). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DX-054 — Old implementation left commented out.** Banned: keeping the superseded code as a commented block above or below its replacement "in case we need it." Defeats: DET-CODE-010. Instead: delete it in the same change — git history recovers it exactly — and note the replacement in the changelog (DX-112). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-055 — Restructuring untested code with no net.** Banned: beginning structural changes in an area with no test coverage and no characterization tests, on the strength of reading the code carefully. Defeats: DET-CODE-013. Instead: pin current behavior with characterization tests first, in their own commit, then refactor under them (DX-102). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-051 — Suite-green invariant (automated).** Verifies: DX-101, DX-102, DX-105. Check: run the project's full test suite on the base commit and on the refactoring branch (`<test-command>` per stack.md, e.g. `npm test`); compare results, and list modified test files: `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD -- '*test*' '*spec*' 'tests/'`. Pass: identical pass/fail sets on both runs and zero test files modified. Fail: block shipment; the change is reclassified or the behavior restored. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-052 — Public surface diff (automated).** Verifies: DX-109. Check: diff the exported surface between base and branch — for a library, the generated type/symbol listing; for an API, the OpenAPI contract (`git diff <base>...HEAD -- openapi.yaml` or the project's contract snapshot). Pass: the surface diff is empty. Fail: block shipment; move the surface change to legacy-migration (branch by abstraction / parallel change). Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-053 — Commit separation audit (automated).** Verifies: DX-103, DX-110. Check: `git log --format='%h %s' <base>..HEAD` — every commit in the change is a single-type change (`refactor:` commits contain no behavior change; no `feat:`/`fix:` commit is interleaved inside the refactoring range), and per-commit size stays reviewable: `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD` shows no single commit rewriting a whole module. Pass: clean separation, no mixed commits. Fail: block shipment; split the commits and resubmit. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-054 — Characterization-first ordering (automated).** Verifies: DX-102. Check: for any module the change restructures that lacked coverage at base, `git log --format='%h %s' --reverse <base>..HEAD -- <module>` shows a test-only commit adding characterization tests for that module before the first structural commit touching it. Pass: ordering holds for every previously untested module. Fail: block shipment; write and land the characterization tests first. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-055 — Deletion and step review (manual).** Verifies: DX-104, DX-112. Check: read the full diff; confirm each commit maps to one named catalog transformation, every superseded implementation is deleted (search the diff and the resulting files for large commented-out blocks), and the change description names the design pressure answered (DX-107). Pass: all three confirmed. Fail: warn once; on repeat, block shipment and split or complete the deletion. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Refactoring changes structure, never behavior — anything else gets a new name.
- No net, no refactoring: characterization tests come first.
- Two hats: never refactor and change behavior in the same commit.
- Red suite means back up one step — never push through, never edit the test.
- Extract at the third occurrence, delete the old code in the same change.

## Checklist

- [ ] Full suite was green on the base commit before the first structural step (DX-102, G-DX-051).
- [ ] Previously untested areas got characterization tests in a preceding, separate commit (DX-102, G-DX-054).
- [ ] No test file is modified anywhere in this change (DX-106, G-DX-051).
- [ ] Every commit is a single named transformation; no feature or fix is mixed in (DX-103, DX-104, G-DX-053).
- [ ] Public surface diff (symbols / OpenAPI) is empty (DX-109, G-DX-052).
- [ ] The change description names the design pressure answered (DX-107).
- [ ] No abstraction was extracted before its third occurrence (DX-108).
- [ ] All superseded code is deleted, none commented out (DX-112, G-DX-055).
- [ ] Suite result after the change matches the base run exactly, recorded in progress.md (G-DX-051).

# tech-debt

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://learningloop.io/glossary/technical-debt ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/workflowsOfRefactoring/fallback.html ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: the debt register is built from shortcuts, workarounds, and TODO/FIXME markers found in the project's own codebase, inspected directly; it records debt rather than consuming another skill's output. It feeds refactoring and legacy-migration.
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, legacy-migration

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a shortcut, workaround, duplication, or stale toggle is being introduced or discovered; TODO/FIXME markers exist in the codebase; a release or iteration plan is being drawn up and repayment capacity must be allocated; the debt register is due its review.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work is the repayment itself (use refactoring for behavior-preserving cleanup, legacy-migration for replacing a system in slices), or the item is a defect in current behavior rather than a known shortcut (track it as a bug, not debt).
- **Cross-reference:** the commented-out-code pattern banned here as BAN-DX-042 is also banned at refactor time in refactoring (BAN-DX-054); the two entries cover the same pattern in different moments.

## Rules

1. **DX-081 — One register, one record.** Every known item of technical debt is a numbered entry (DEBT-NNN) in the project's single debt register, `docs/tech-debt.md`. Debt known only from chat, memory, or code comments is not recorded debt — it is invisible debt, and invisible debt is never scheduled.
2. **DX-082 — Complete fields at birth.** Every entry carries, from the moment it is created: location (file/module), Fowler quadrant (deliberate/inadvertent × prudent/reckless), the interest it charges, a named owner, a repayment trigger (a date, or the next feature/release touching that area), and the date incurred. An entry missing any field is incomplete and fails G-DX-042.
3. **DX-083 — Deliberate debt is registered in the same change that incurs it.** A shortcut taken on purpose gets its register entry in the same pull request that merges the shortcut. Registering it "later" is how deliberate debt becomes inadvertent.
4. **DX-084 — Deliberate + reckless is not a permitted category.** A shortcut with no repayment trigger and no plan is not debt, it is an unmade decision: the review blocks it, or the scope is cut until the work can be done properly.
5. **DX-085 — Interest is stated concretely.** The interest field names the work the debt slows or the risk it creates, in observable terms ("every billing change requires the same edit in three duplicated places"). "Code is messy," "needs cleanup," and similar phrases are not interest statements and are rejected at review.
6. **DX-086 — Code markers must reference the register.** Every `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK`, or `XXX` comment carries a register reference, e.g. `TODO(DEBT-123): …`. A marker with no reference is either fixed in place, converted into a register entry with a reference, or deleted in the same change that touches it. Core functionality is never deferred to a marker — a marker may only defer minor, already-working-around items.
7. **DX-087 — Temporary means an expiry.** Every workaround and hack carries its repayment trigger as its expiry. When a trigger fires (the date passes, or work touches the area), repayment is scheduled into the next plan — the trigger firing is the scheduling event, not a reminder to update the date.
8. **DX-088 — Inadvertent debt is logged as a defect to schedule.** Debt discovered while reading or changing code (reckless shortcuts, rotted patterns, undocumented workarounds) is entered in the register the day it is found, classified inadvertent, and scheduled like a defect. It is neither silently fixed opportunistically inside an unrelated change nor noted and forgotten.
9. **DX-089 — Repayment is a standing capacity slice.** Each iteration or release plan reserves a stated slice of capacity for repayment (the project names its figure, e.g. one item or a fixed share of the plan) before new feature work is allocated. Repayment is never negotiated item-by-item against features at planning time.
10. **DX-090 — Closure requires a merged change.** An entry is closed only by a merged change that removes the debt, and the closure records the date and the change reference. Editing an entry away, or deciding it "no longer matters," is not closure; an item the project consciously accepts permanently is reclassified as a recorded accepted-risk decision, with the decider named.
11. **DX-091 — The register is reviewed on a cadence and reported.** The register is reviewed at least once per release (or monthly, whichever is sooner): triggers checked against today, owners confirmed live, expired items scheduled. The open-item count and the age of the oldest open item are reported in progress.md like any other project metric.
12. **DX-092 — Stale flags are a debt class.** Every feature flag/toggle is a register entry (or register-listed) with an owner and a removal trigger, classified by its toggle type (release, experiment, ops, permissioning). A flag whose trigger has passed is debt in default and is scheduled for removal before new flags are added in the same area.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-041 — Bare TODO/FIXME marker.** Banned: a `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK`, or `XXX` comment with no register reference, owner, or trigger. Defeats: DET-CODE-011. Instead: fix it now, or create the register entry and write `// TODO(DEBT-123): validate postcode format — see register` (DX-086). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-042 — Commented-out code kept as memory.** Banned: leaving a superseded implementation commented out "in case we need it" instead of deleting it and, if the reason matters, recording the decision in the register or decision log. Defeats: DET-CODE-010. Instead: delete it — version control is the archive — and note the replacement in the changelog (DX-090). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-043 — Duplication merged as the permanent solution, off-register.** Banned: copy-pasting logic into a second or third location and merging it with no register entry recording the duplication and its consolidation trigger. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Instead: either extract the shared function now, or register the duplication as deliberate + prudent debt with the trigger "next change to any copy" (DX-083, DX-085). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-044 — Register entry deleted to close it.** Banned: removing or rewriting a register entry so the debt disappears from the record without a merged fix. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: close entries only under DX-090 — merged change reference recorded, or a named accepted-risk reclassification. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-045 — Stub shipped as done, gap relabeled "debt" off-register.** Banned: presenting a placeholder or stub as the finished feature and calling the missing behavior "technical debt" without a register entry. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Instead: the feature is not done — either implement it, or ship it visibly incomplete with the gap registered, triggered, and owned (DX-082, DX-083). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-041 — Marker-reference lint (automated).** Verifies: DX-086. Check: `grep -rnE '\b(TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX)\b' --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git . | grep -vE '(TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX)\(DEBT-[0-9]+\)' | grep -vE '(samples|templates|examples|docs|locales)/'` — instructional fill-in prompts in copy-and-edit templates are excluded per DET-CODE-011. Pass: no output (every marker carries a register reference). Fail: block shipment until each hit is fixed, registered, or deleted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-042 — Register completeness check (automated).** Verifies: DX-081, DX-082. Check: parse the register table in `docs/tech-debt.md` (columns: ID, location, quadrant, interest, owner, trigger, incurred) and assert no cell is empty: `awk -F'|' 'NR>2 {for(i=2;i<=8;i++) if($i ~ /^[[:space:]]*$/) {print "incomplete:", $2; bad=1}} END {exit bad}' docs/tech-debt.md`. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block shipment; complete the fields before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-043 — Cross-reference and expiry check (automated).** Verifies: DX-086, DX-087. Check: extract register IDs from code (`grep -rhoE 'DEBT-[0-9]+' --exclude-dir=.git . | sort -u`) and from the register's ID column; `comm` the two lists — code references with no register entry, and register entries with no code reference where a location is in code, are reported; entries whose trigger date is past are listed. Pass: zero dangling references; past-trigger entries appear on the next plan. Fail: block shipment on dangling references; warn on past triggers until scheduled. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-044 — Register audit (manual).** Verifies: DX-088, DX-091. Check: at the release/monthly review, sample at least five open entries (or all, if fewer): confirm each owner is still the right owner, each trigger is in the future or scheduled, and each interest statement still describes reality; record open count and oldest-item age in progress.md. Pass: every sampled entry verified and metrics recorded. Fail: warn; correct entries and re-run before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-045 — Closure audit (manual).** Verifies: DX-090. Check: list every entry closed since the last release; for each, open the recorded change reference and confirm the merged change actually removes the debt at the entry's location; diff the register against its previous version (`git log -p docs/tech-debt.md`) and confirm no entry vanished without a closure record. Pass: zero unexplained closures or deletions. Fail: block shipment; restore the entry or record a proper closure. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- If it is not in the register, it is not scheduled — it is invisible.
- Deliberate debt is registered in the same change that incurs it.
- "Temporary" without a trigger and an owner is permanent.
- Interest is concrete work slowed or risk created — never "messy."
- Entries close by merged changes, never by editing the register.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every new shortcut from this change has a register entry created in the same change (DX-083).
- [ ] Every entry has location, quadrant, concrete interest, owner, trigger, and incurred date (DX-082, G-DX-042).
- [ ] No deliberate + reckless item was merged — blocked or scope cut (DX-084).
- [ ] Marker lint passes: every TODO/FIXME/HACK carries a DEBT reference (DX-086, G-DX-041).
- [ ] No core functionality is deferred to a code marker (DX-086).
- [ ] Inadvertent debt found during this work is logged and scheduled (DX-088).
- [ ] This plan reserves its standing repayment slice before feature allocation (DX-089).
- [ ] Closures since the last release each cite a merged change; register metrics are in progress.md (DX-090, DX-091, G-DX-045).

# versioning

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://semver.org/ ; https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/ ; https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/
- **Depends on:** changelog
- **Feeds into:** dependency-management

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** cutting any release of a library, package, API, or deployed app; choosing the next version number; deprecating or removing a public feature; withdrawing a bad release; setting up a project's release process.
- **Do NOT use when:** versioning an HTTP API's URL/contract scheme itself (use api-versioning in D2 — this skill supplies the SemVer contract and deprecation window it builds on), or recording what changed in prose (use changelog in D10 — this skill governs the number, the tag, and their consistency).

## Rules

1. **DX-141 — SemVer 2.0.0 is the public contract.** Every published package, library, and API carries a version of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with SemVer precedence rules: MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for backward-compatible functionality, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. No other numbering scheme (dates, codenames, "final") is used for the same artifact.
2. **DX-142 — One source of truth for the version.** The version string lives in exactly one place — the package manifest or the git tag, as the project declares — and every other appearance (docs, banners, generated files, `--version` output) is read or generated from that source. No file is hand-edited to "also" update the version.
3. **DX-143 — The bump is derived, not chosen.** The next bump is computed from the Conventional Commits in the range since the last release tag: any `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer or `!` → MAJOR; else any `feat:` → MINOR; else PATCH. The highest signal wins, and the release notes state the derivation. A bump that disagrees with the derivation is a defect.
4. **DX-144 — Breaking changes force a major bump and a migration note.** Any incompatible change to the public API — removed or renamed symbols, changed signatures, changed defaults or behavior consumers rely on — ships only under a new MAJOR version, and its changelog entry carries a migration note saying what consumers must change. There is no "small breaking change" exception.
5. **DX-145 — Deprecation precedes removal.** A public feature is marked deprecated in at least one MINOR release (libraries/APIs) before it is removed in a MAJOR release, announced in the changelog's Deprecated section with the replacement named. Removal without a prior deprecation release is a process failure, not a shortcut.
6. **DX-146 — Pre-1.0 is an explicit, declared state.** While the major version is 0, the project states in its README that anything may change; within 0.x, incompatible changes bump MINOR and compatible features bump PATCH. Version 1.0.0 is cut when the public API becomes a real commitment consumers are invited to depend on — not when the code feels old enough.
7. **DX-147 — Pre-release and build metadata follow the SemVer grammar.** Pre-release suffixes are dot-separated identifiers (`1.0.0-alpha.1`, `1.0.0-rc.2`) with no leading zeros in numeric identifiers; build metadata (`+build.5`) never affects precedence and is never the only difference between two published artifacts. Invented suffixes outside the grammar (`-final`, `-new`, `-v2`) are invalid versions.
8. **DX-148 — A released version is immutable.** Once a version is tagged and published, its code and artifacts are never modified, re-tagged, or republished. A fix ships as a new PATCH version. If the tag must move because the release was cut in error before publication, that fact is recorded in progress.md with the reason — after publication, never.
9. **DX-149 — A release is a consistent triple.** Each release produces, in one release commit: a git tag `vX.Y.Z`, the manifest version set to the identical string (without the `v`), and the top CHANGELOG version heading with the same number and an ISO 8601 date. If any of the three disagrees, the release is not done.
10. **DX-150 — The changelog is the consumer record of versions.** Releases move entries from `[Unreleased]` into a new version section, grouped by the six Keep a Changelog types (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security), written for consumers — what changed for them — with breaking changes marked in place. Entries are added under `[Unreleased]` as work lands, not reconstructed from memory at release time.
11. **DX-151 — Yanked releases stay in history, marked.** A withdrawn release is marked `[YANKED]` in the changelog with the date and reason, and its tag remains. Deleting the section, the tag, or the artifact record so the version "never happened" destroys the trace consumers need when they are pinned to it.
12. **DX-152 — Deployed apps version for traceability.** A deployed web app still tags every production deployment and keeps the changelog; its version is an internal traceability device (deployment → tag → exact commit), so bump rules may relax but DX-148 and DX-149 do not. Every bug report and incident note cites the deployed version or tag it was observed on.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-071 — Silent re-tag or republish.** Banned: moving a version tag to a different commit, or replacing a published artifact, so the same version number names different code. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: publish the fix as 2.3.2 with its own tag and changelog entry (DX-148). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-072 — Breaking change under a minor or patch bump.** Banned: shipping an incompatible API change while bumping only MINOR or PATCH, because the change "feels small." Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: bump MAJOR and write the migration note (DX-144). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-073 — Version hand-edited in several places.** Banned: updating the version by editing the manifest, a source constant, and the docs independently, so the copies can disagree. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: keep one source of truth and generate or read every other display from it (DX-142). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-074 — Non-SemVer release identity.** Banned: releasing under an identity that is not a valid SemVer version — `latest`, `final`, `1.0`, `2.0-new`, or a date — for a versioned artifact. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: assign the next derived SemVer version and tag it (DX-141, DX-143, DX-147). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-075 — Erasing a withdrawn release.** Banned: deleting a yanked version's changelog section, tag, or release record instead of marking it withdrawn. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: mark it `[YANKED]` with the date and reason, tag intact (DX-151). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-071 — Version triple equality (automated).** Verifies: DX-142, DX-149. Check: extract the manifest version (`node -p "require('./package.json').version"` or the ecosystem equivalent), the newest tag (`git describe --tags --abbrev=0`), and the top CHANGELOG version heading; assert all three are the identical version string. Pass: exact match. Fail: block shipment; fix the out-of-line copy from the source of truth, never by editing all three by hand. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-072 — Bump derivation check (automated).** Verifies: DX-143. Check: run commit lint (commitlint with the Conventional Commits config) over `git log <last-tag>..HEAD`, compute the derived bump from the commit types, and compare it with the bump actually taken between the last tag and the candidate version. Pass: lint clean and derived bump equals actual bump. Fail: block shipment; either correct the version or correct the commit record — never ship a number the history does not justify. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-073 — Breaking-change / major-bump check (automated).** Verifies: DX-144. Check: diff the public contract against the last release (OpenAPI diff for APIs, exported-symbol diff for libraries); if the diff reports a breaking change, assert the candidate version's MAJOR is exactly one greater and MINOR/PATCH are zero. Pass: no breaking change, or major bumped. Fail: block shipment until the bump is corrected and the migration note exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-074 — Immutability and grammar check (automated).** Verifies: DX-147, DX-148. Check: validate the candidate version against the official SemVer regular expression from semver.org, and confirm every existing release tag still points at the commit recorded for it at its release (compare `git rev-parse vX.Y.Z^{commit}` against the release record in progress.md). Pass: version is valid SemVer and no tag has moved. Fail: block shipment; a moved tag is restored or the change is shipped as a new version. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-075 — Release record review (manual).** Verifies: DX-145, DX-150, DX-151. Check: read the new changelog section as a consumer: entries grouped by the six types, breaking changes marked with migration notes, anything removed was announced as Deprecated at least one minor release earlier, and any withdrawn release in the period is marked `[YANKED]` with a reason. Pass: all four hold. Fail: warn and complete the record before the next release; a missing prior deprecation blocks the removal itself. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- The version is a contract, not a mood: derive the bump from the commits.
- One source of truth — tag, manifest, and changelog are the same string or the release is not done.
- Breaking change means major bump plus a migration note. No exceptions for "small" breaks.
- Published means immutable: fixes ship as a new version, never a moved tag.
- Yanked is marked, never erased.

## Checklist

- [ ] The candidate version is valid SemVer, including any pre-release/build suffixes (DX-141, DX-147, G-DX-074).
- [ ] The bump matches the derivation from the commit range since the last tag (DX-143, G-DX-072).
- [ ] Any breaking change has a major bump and a migration note in the changelog (DX-144, G-DX-073).
- [ ] Anything removed was deprecated at least one minor release earlier (DX-145, G-DX-075).
- [ ] Tag, manifest, and changelog heading are the identical version string (DX-149, G-DX-071).
- [ ] No existing tag moved and no published artifact was replaced (DX-148, G-DX-074).
- [ ] The changelog section is grouped by the six types and written for consumers (DX-150).
- [ ] Any withdrawn release is marked `[YANKED]` with a reason, not deleted (DX-151).
